 both the public and City staff safe, the public will be permitted to physically attend

City Council  Wednesday, February 2, 2022
  The safety and well-being of employees and the public remains the City's top priority. The
 City of Palmdale appreciates your patience and understanding during these challenging
 times.

 The City Council is making every effort to follow the spirit and intent of the Brown Act and
 other applicable laws regulating the conduct of public meetings in order to maximize
 transparency and public access.

 In accordance with the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, if you require a disability-
 related modification or accommodation to participate in this meeting, please contact the
 City Clerk’s Office at (661) 267-5151 at least 72 hours prior to the meeting.

 If you require oral Spanish translation, please contact the City Clerk’s Office at (661) 267-
 5151 at least 72 hours prior to the meeting.

 Your courtesy is requested to help our meetings run smoothly. If you’ll be kind enough to
 follow these simple rules, we can make the best possible use of your time and ours:

  Please refrain from public displays or outbursts, such as unsolicited applause,
  comments, cheering, foul language or obscenities.
  Any disruptive activities that substantially interfere with the ability of the City Council
  to carry out its meeting will not be permitted and offenders will be asked to leave the
  meeting.
  Please turn off/mute your cell phones and mobile devices.

   City Council Staff Report
DATE:  FEBRUARY 2, 2022
TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL
FROM:  CITY MANAGER’S OFFICE – FINANCE DIVISION
DISTRICT:  ALL
SUBJECT:  RECEIVE AND FILE THE MONTHLY AND QUARTERLY
  INVESTMENT ACTIVITY REPORTS FOR DECEMBER 2021.

ISSUE
Receive and file the monthly and quarterly investment activity reports for December
2021.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council accept the monthly and quarterly investment
activity reports for City of Palmdale and Successor Agency for December 2021.

BACKGROUND
Pursuant to Section 16 of the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency Investment
Policy, the City Treasurer shall prepare and present monthly and quarterly reports on
investments to the City Manager/Executive Director and the City Council/Directors. The
reports shall detail the type of investment, name of the issuer, purchase date, date of
maturity, amount of deposit, and rate of interest. This information shall be provided for
all City and Successor Agency pooled investments, as well as for Certificates of
Participation, Revenue Bonds, Tax Allocation Bonds, Assessment Districts and
Community Facilities District accounts which are managed by outside Fiscal Agents.
The monthly and quarterly reports provide a synopsis of the investment activity for the
City of Palmdale and Successor Agency. The reports provide information on assets,
allocations, average maturities, yields, and book valuations.
The interest rates presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this
report.
The market values presented for pooled City and Successor Agency investments are
based on closing prices for the related investment as of the date of this report. This
information was obtained from the Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg Financial Markets,
Capital Market Finances, or other reliable source of market prices.

DISCUSSION
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Monthly and Quarterly Reports on Investments
February 2, 2022
Page 2

Compliance with Investment Policy

For December, the invested portfolio amount for the City of Palmdale totaled
$232,320,784, an increase of $1,402,465 from the previous month and an increase of
$42,625,052 in comparison to last year. The increase in overall portfolio balance from
the previous month is a result of interest earned on investments during the month. There
were no maturities of securities during the month of December. The City purchased a
total of eleven new securities during the month for a total of $71,103,743. Funds for
these purchases were previously being held in the City and the PCA LAIF accounts.

The par value of Successor Agency’s portfolio as of December was $5,740,875. The
balance decreased by $1,012,631 from last month due to quarterly debt service
payments made during the month.

All investments meet criteria appropriate to Section 8 of the Investment Policy. The
portfolios are based on a combination of various investments, including CDs, Corporate
Notes, U.S. Treasury Securities and Government Agency Paper, each adhering to
portfolio percentage limitations.

The Finance Division is the custodian for the City and Successor Agency’s investment
portfolio and follows the three main principles of both entity’s investment policy to 1)
Investment in financial instruments that mitigate the risk of monetary losses stemming
from market fluctuations; 2) Establish and maintain a portfolio that has sufficient liquidity
to allow the City and Successor Agency to meet all anticipated cash requirements; and
3) Seek out investment instruments that provide a competitive market rate of return.

Liquidity

One core approach the Finance Division focuses on, is providing liquidity to measure up
to the City and Successor Agency’s operational requirements. Thus, the Finance
Department is currently investing in two pooled funds, LAIF and CAMP. These are
intended for the daily operational activities, used for economic uncertainties and
maintenance needs. The pooled funds provide a higher liquidity ratio to ensure the City
and Successor Agency meet cash flow requirements.

Total LAIF balance for the City of Palmdale is $64,967,143 compared to November’s
balance of $134,967,143. The decrease in balance is due to funds being withdrawn from
LAIF and used for the purchase of eleven new securities during the month.

Successor Agency LAIF balance at the end of June was $3,695,024, a 28.8 percent
decrease from June, and a decrease of $1,500,000 from the prior month. The decrease
in balance for the year is due to funds being withdrawn from LAIF account to be used to
support current financial obligations and debt service payments.

CAMP’s balance for City of Palmdale is $248,736 compared to November’s balance of
$248,725. The slight increase is due to interest received during the month.

The interest rates presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this
report. As of December 31, 2021, the interest rates for LAIF and CAMP investments
were at .21 percent and .05 percent, respectively. By comparison, the LAIF and CAMP
interest rates at the end of November were at .20 percent and .05 percent. Both rates
have been steadily declining since March 2020. This time last year, LAIF and CAMP
rates were at 0.54 percent and .12, respectively.

The chart above shows both the Local Agency Investment Fund and California
Management Program’s average monthly yields beginning March 2021 through
December 2021. The graph depicts the prolonged period of declining rates and shows
that rates have begun to level off from September through December 2021.

We anticipate that rates will remain low in the upcoming months, with slight fluctuations,
considering the economic impacts of COVID. Overall, LAIF shows better performance
than CAMP in interest rates. The difference between the performance of the two funds
is partly due to the varying pool characteristics. CAMP’s portfolio composition is much
more subject to market volatility, resulting in performance variation.

Diversity

The Finance Division aims to diversify the investment portfolios to avoid incurring
unreasonable and avoidable risks regarding specific security types or individual financial
institutions.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Monthly and Quarterly Reports on Investments
February 2, 2022
Page 4

City of Palmdale and Successor Agency’s investment portfolios remain strongly
diversified. The monthly and quarterly reports include all investments held by both
entities and current book values as of December 31, 2021.

In December, there were no securities that were called or matured. The City purchased
a total of eleven new securities, totaling $71,103,743. Five of those securities are U.S.
Treasury Notes, and six are Government Agency paper.

It is anticipated that both the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency will have sufficient
moneys to meet its expenditure requirements for the next 6 months as we continue to
monitor any financial impact due to the Coronavirus pandemic.

Attached are summaries of the investments on the City of Palmdale and Successor
Agency’s books as of December 31, 2021.

FISCAL IMPACT
There is no fiscal impact associated with the recommended actions for this report.

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-016, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale approving and authorizing the execution and delivery of a Supplemental
Agreement No. 5 to Amended and Restated Fiscal Agent Agreement related to
Community Facilities District No. 93-1(Ritter Ranch), and authorizing related actions.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-016, a Resolution of the City Council of the City
  of Palmdale approving and authorizing the execution and delivery of a
  Supplemental Agreement No. 5 to Amended and Restated Fiscal Agent
  Agreement related to Community Facilities District No. 93-1(Ritter Ranch), and
  authorizing related actions.

BACKGROUND
In 1994, the City Council formed the City of Palmdale Community Facilities District No.
93-1 (Ritter Ranch), and in 1995 the City issued special tax bonds for the Community
Facilities District to finance various public infrastructure improvements within and in the
vicinity of the proposed Ritter Ranch development. The prior owner of the Ritter Ranch
property, Ritter Holdings LLC, failed to make required special tax payments due in
February of 2020, and its lender, Preston Hollow Capital, LLC (Preston Hollow), which
also is the owner of the special tax bonds, foreclosed on the Ritter Ranch property and
became the owner of the Ritter Ranch property and all of the rights and interests of Ritter
Holdings, LLC under agreements with the City and others related to Ritter Ranch. Preston
Hollow subsequently transferred the Ritter Ranch property to RdR Development
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-016
February 2, 2022
Page 2

Holdings, LLC, a Delaware limited liability company (“RdR”), of which Preston Hollow is
the sole member.

On September 1, 2020, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 2020-091, pursuant to
which, at the request of Preston Hollow, it approved a supplement to the agreement
pursuant to which the special tax bonds were issued, to defer payments otherwise due
on the special tax bonds during the period from March 1, 2020 to and including March 1,
2022 to allow time for Preston Hollow and RdR to determine the actions needed to
commence development of the Ritter Ranch property. That Resolution also approved a
Deposit Agreement (A-7107) between the City and Preston Hollow (the “Deposit
Agreement”) pursuant to which Preston Hollow advanced funds to pay costs of the City
and its consultants related to requests by it and RdR relative to the development of the
Ritter Ranch property. To date, Preston Hollow had advanced a total of $527,096.94 to
the City to be used as provided in the Deposit Agreement, including City actions related
to the current request to process a supplement to the agreement pursuant to which the
special tax bonds were issued.

DISCUSSION
Since their obtaining ownership of the Ritter Ranch property, Preston Hollow and RdR
have proceeded to take actions necessary to restart the development of Ritter Ranch.
Preston Hollow and RdR have asked that the City agree to again amend the documents
for the special tax bonds to defer bond payments otherwise due for the next year in order
to allow them additional time to take the actions needed to continue the development of
the property.

The City Council is now requested to approve a supplement to the agreement governing
the special tax bonds to defer payments on the bonds. The supplement has been
prepared by the City’s bond counsel, Quint & Thimmig LLP, and has been reviewed by
City Finance Department Staff and the City Attorney.

FISCAL IMPACT
There is no impact to the General Fund as the bond payment obligation rests solely with
the current property owner, RdR Development Holdings, LLC, of which Preston Hollow
is the sole member. The deferral of the bonds payment would trigger Community
Facilities Districts 93-1 (Ritter Ranch) to stop levying the property tax and in turn not to
make the bond payment to the owner of the special tax bonds, Preston Hollow which a
sole member of property owner entity. As such, no budget is requested for this action.

The fiscal impact to consider are the costs of City Staff and consultants related to
requests by the bond owner and the current owner of the Ritter Ranch property for City
actions in respect of the development of the property in the Ritter Ranch Community
Facilities District No. 93-1 and otherwise related to the outstanding bonds. The current
owner of the outstanding bonds that have been issued by the City for Community

Facilities District No. 93-1 has deposited funds in the amount $527,096.94 with the City
to pay for the costs from September, 2020 to November, 2021. The significant portion
of the $527,096.94 deposit was disbursed to consultants, primarily attorneys, for the
services provided in connection with the requests by the prior owner, Suncal. Currently,
the remaining deposit funds is approximately $307,000. As the deposited funds are
depleted, staffs will request the additional funds as necessary.

ISSUE
Approve an Agreement for Legal Services Between the City of Palmdale and Silver &
Right, LLP (A-7783) in the Amount of $500,000.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Approve an Agreement for Legal Services Between the City of Palmdale and
  Silver & Wright, LLP (A-7783) in the Amount of $500,000.

BACKGROUND
The law firm of Silver & Wright, LLP has represented the City since 2016, providing
general advice regarding code enforcement and prosecuting nuisance abatement
actions on behalf of the City. Silver & Wright, LLP has been successful abating
nuisance properties within the City and routinely obtains full cost recovery for the City.

DISCUSSION
The most recent contract for legal services with Silver & Wright, LLP (A-6400) ended in
September 2021. Because there were no extensions available to the previous contract
(A-6400), a new contract is required between the City of Palmdale and Silver & Wright,
LLP to cover the resolution of pending matters and allow the City to use the law firm on
future matters.

Staff recommends that the City Council approve the Agreement for Legal Services
between the City of Palmdale and Silver & Wright, LLP (A-7783) in the amount of
$500,000.

ISSUE
Approve Agreement with Management Partners, Inc. to Provide Consulting Services
Regarding Misdemeanor Prosecutions within the City of Palmdale.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Approve Agreement with Management Partners, Inc. to Provide Consulting
  Services Regarding Misdemeanor Prosecutions within the City of Palmdale.
  2. Authorize appropriation of funds from General Fund unappropriated fund
  balance.

BACKGROUND
At present, the City Attorney’s office has significant prosecutorial authority to prosecute
violations of the Palmdale Municipal Code and Ordinances. Palmdale Municipal Code
Section 2.06.060 provides that the City Attorney shall have the power to “initiate all
proceedings in law or equity for the criminal or civil enforcement of all City ordinances
and for the defense of the City in all legal actions.” PMC 2.06.060.B. In practice, these
violations can be charged, or filed, as administrative actions, infractions or
misdemeanors. The associated penalty for such is graduated accordingly. California
Code of Civil Procedure §731 authorizes a municipalities City Attorney’s office to
prosecute public nuisance actions in the name of the People of the State of California.
See, California Code of Civil Procedure §731.

At the City Council meeting on July 13, 2021, the City Attorney provided an
informational item on City prosecutions, noting, in part, that there has been a significant
increase in the number of cases that have been rejected for filing under Special
Directive 20-07, which directed all Deputy District Attorneys to reject for filing, with a few
exceptions, the case types below when submitted by law enforcement for filing:

a) Trespass – Penal Code §602 (a)-(y)*

This report was subsequently received and filed by the City Council.

At the City Council meeting on August 17, 2021, the City Council voted 5-0 and directed
the City Attorney’s Office to hire a consultant to conduct a feasibility study expanding
the capacity of the City Attorney regarding Municipal and Misdemeanor Prosecutions.

DISCUSSION
In response to the City Council’s vote on August 17, 2021, the City Attorney’s Office is
recommending the approval of Management Partners, Inc. to provide consulting
services regarding in-house misdemeanor prosecutions within the City of Palmdale.
Management Partners, Inc. was founded in 1994 with a specific mission to help local
government leaders improve their service to the public. They have previously performed
several City Attorney organizational assessments for cities throughout California
including the City of San Bernardino, City of Fremont, and the City of Berkeley.
As discussed in their proposed scope of work, Management Partners, Inc. has
developed a six-month plan to compare the staffing costs and feasibility of three options
for expanding misdemeanor prosecutions in the City of Palmdale:
  (1) Expanding in-house prosecutions gradually. Create a plan to allow the City
  Attorney’s Office to gradually expand the number and types of prosecutions
  handled under the current organizational structure;
  (2) Establishing an in-house prosecution division. Create a plan that creates a new
  prosecution division in the City Attorney’s Office which will have grater capacity
  than a graduated prosecution option; and
  (3) Contract with another city or private law firm to expand misdemeanor
  prosecution. Create a plan that would analyze the feasibility of contracting with
  another city or a private law firm to handle misdemeanor prosecutions that have
  been declined by the Los Angeles District Attorney.

ISSUE
Approve Supplemental Agreement No. 3 with RSB Group, Inc. for PN 784, Rancho Vista
Park, in the amount of $218,855.81.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Approve Supplemental No. 3 with RSB Group, Inc. for PN 784 Rancho Vista
  Park, in the amount of $218,855.81, Agreement No. A-7149; and

  2. Authorize the transfer of $112,600 of unappropriated park funds into Account
  P0054220; and

  3. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to execute Supplemental Agreement
  No. 3 to Agreement No. A-7149 with RSB Group, Inc., including making minimal
  and/or non-substantive changes.

BACKGROUND
Project No. 784, Rancho Vista Park, was awarded to RSB Group, Inc. in November 2020.
This project is creating a neighborhood park on Town Center Drive, between 35th Street
West and Bolz Ranch Road, adjacent to Los Angeles County Fire Station #136 and
Esperanza Elementary School. The park will include but not be limited to a prefabricated
restroom facility, inclusive playground, small parking lot, an ADA accessible walking path
with lighting, monument sign, picnic areas and shade trees, story time area, drinking
fountain, pet waste station, and therapeutic wellness garden/meditation space.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Amendment No. 3 to PN 784, Rancho Vista Park
February 2, 2022
Page 2

DISCUSSION
This project has two previous Supplemental Agreements that were approved
administratively under authority of City Manager. Supplemental Agreement No. 1
included a variety of changes in scope including, but not limited to materials upgrade,
regrading, additional wiring, and discrepancies resulting from bidding the project prior to
having a fully approved plan set. Supplemental Agreement No. 2 was largely due to the
change in electrical scope after Southern California Edison determined they could not
achieve the specified and approved electrical run, but also included miscellaneous
material/design revisions as recommended by City Maintenance for long-term durability.

This Supplemental Agreement No. 3 includes four (4) changes to the project scope as
outlined below. The 1st change relates to the waterline service connection for the park.
The waterline service connection was not included on the bid set of plans and was
therefore not included in the original bid and contract. The cost for this change includes
the water connection in the street (trenching, piping and appurtenances), traffic control,
and agency coordination.

The 2nd change relates to additional work required to mitigate an elevation discrepancy
with a project storm drain catch basin. After field verification, it was determined that the
elevation of the existing storm drain line that the park connects to was higher than that
taken from existing utility drawings. Due to this discrepancy in elevation, the storm drain
connection required an elevation adjustment and construction changes to the catch basin
and the storm drain line.

The 3rd change relates to supply chain problems with the specified, and contracted,
playground equipment. Replacement equipment was secured. However, a design
change required by this new equipment necessitated additional fibar and concrete border
curb. The layout with the least impact to the project was determined in collaboration with
the landscape architect, playground equipment manufacturer, and contractor. The
approved plans did not provide a detail showing the curb depth necessary for this use
zone clearance, necessitating additional fibar cushioning. The additional cost includes
concrete, fibar cushion, and the labor to accomplish the proposed solution.

The 4th change relates to the construction of the seat wall adjacent to a retaining wall.
City Inspection staff paused construction of the seat wall with concerns that the seat wall
might be required to be tied to the adjacent retaining wall. Upon consulting with the
Design Engineer of Record, this requirement was determined to be unnecessary. The
seat wall construction was able to resume, but the time spent evaluating the requirement
created a delay in the work which was then further delayed due to rain. Additional costs
for the rental of concrete forms were incurred by the contractor and the City negotiated to
cover half of these rental costs.

SUBJECT:  ADOPT RESOLUTION NO. CC 2022-018, A RESOLUTION OF THE
  CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE AUTHORIZING
  SUBMISSION OF A NOTIFICATION OF THE CITY’S INTENT TO
  COMPLY WITH SENATE BILL 619, TO THE STATE DEPARTMENT
  OF RESOURCES RECYCLING AND RECOVERY (CalRecycle)

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-018, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale authorizing submission of a Notification of the City’s Intent to Comply with
Senate Bill (SB) 619, to the State Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery
(CalRecycle).

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-018, authorizing submission of a Notification of the City’s
Intent to Comply with SB 619, to the State Department of Resources Recycling and
Recovery (CalRecycle).

BACKGROUND

The State has committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions under California’s
Short-Lived Climate Pollutant Reduction Strategy also known as Senate Bill (SB) 1383.
The State’s target is to reduce organic waste disposal by 75 percent by 2025.
Additionally, the State is looking to recover 20 percent of edible food waste that currently
is being disposed for consumption by those in need.

SB 1383 was adopted in 2016 and regulations were approved in November 2020.
Regulations took effect January 1, 2022. However, due to the challenges many local
governments faced during the COVID-19 pandemic; Governor Newsom signed SB 619
into law to support local governments as they design and implement successful organic
waste recycling programs.

SB 619 authorizes CalRecycle to waive civil penalties if a jurisdiction submits a
Notification of Intent to Comply for some or all of the applicable regulatory requirements
(waiver will only apply to the requirements outlined in the application), implements a plan
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Approval of Resolution No. CC 2022-018
Date of Meeting: February 2, 2022
Page 2

to correct their violations, and is approved. Jurisdictions must successfully implement
the plan to correct their shortfalls for compliance with the requirements that take effect
during the 2022 calendar year, continuing the compliance deadline to the 2023 calendar
year. To avoid penalties, the jurisdiction must adopt a resolution to certify the contents
and timeline of the Notification of Intent to Comply. The application along with
Notification to Comply and resolution must be submitted to CalRecycle by March 1,
2022. SB 619 does not provide an exemption from compliance; it only allows a
deference of compliance for a year. CalRecycle has indicated that if a jurisdiction does
not follow-through with its approved proposed actions and schedule as outlined in the
notification, then they may rescind approval and impose penalties for violations
occurring retroactively to the date of violation.

DISCUSSION

Notice of Intent to Comply includes a description of the continuing violations, an
explanation of the reason why the City is unable to comply, a description of the impacts
of the COVID-19 pandemic on compliance, and a description of the proposed actions
the City will take to remedy the violations.

When the City put its Franchise Agreement out to bid and awarded it to Waste
Management in 2017, the City worked with Waste Management to address organics,
recognizing the State was going to implement more stringent requirements. The
program started with providing organic waste collection services to local businesses.
Many local businesses have been educated about the upcoming changes and site visits
have been conducted to assess their waste generation activities and space available to
evaluate what size containers and frequency of service they will need to be in
compliance.

On January 29, 2020, the City received a Notice of Mandatory Commercial Organics
Recycling (MORe) Program Implementation Gap and shortly after that a Notice of
Mandatory Commercial Recycling (MCR) Program Implementation Gap from
CalRecycle. As a result, the City implemented the following programs to comply:
education and outreach, enforcement, service tracking, and compliance monitoring.
The City also had to be an early implementor of an enforceable ordinance that would
require commercial and multifamily complexes to recycle their organic waste. Pursuant
to the ordinance, if found to be non-compliant the generator would potentially face a
penalty.

The City is in negotiations with Waste Management working on a Franchise Agreement
amendment to be in full compliance with SB 1383, which will include several items
recommended by CalRecycle’s model agreement and ordinance. Staff is also working
with Waste Management on identifying an option and long-term solution for addressing
all organic waste generated in the City.

FISCAL IMPACT

If the City does not submit Notification of Intent to Comply and the City is found to have
violated SB 1383 regulations by CalRecycle, the City may face penalties starting from
$500 up to a maximum $10,000 per violation, per day. The penalties can be combined;
therefore, depending on the number and severity of the violations, the penalties could
potentially be up to $10,000 per day of violation.

CalRecycle is providing this optional form as a convenience to assist jurisdictions (counties, cities, a
county and city, or special districts providing solid waste collection services) for purposes of
submitting a notification of intent to comply to CalRecycle [see Public Resources Code (PRC)
section 42652.5(c)].

A jurisdiction may submit a notification of intent to comply if it is facing continuing violations of the
Short-lived Climate Pollutants: Organic Waste Reductions requirements in Title 14 California Code
of Regulations (14 CCR). The written notification of intent to comply, adopted by resolution of the
jurisdiction’s governing body, shall be sent to CalRecycle no later than March 1, 2022, to
NOIC@CalRecycle.ca.gov.

A jurisdiction shall, at minimum, include the following in its notification:
  1. A description, with specificity, of the continuing violations.
  2. A detailed explanation of the reasons, supported by documentation, why the local jurisdiction
  is unable to comply.
  3. A description of the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on compliance.
  4. A description of the proposed actions the local jurisdiction will take to remedy the violations
  within the timelines established in 14 CCR section 18996.2 with a proposed schedule for
  doing so. The proposed actions shall be tailored to remedy the violations in a timely manner.

Upon approval by CalRecycle of a jurisdiction’s notification and implementation of the intent to
comply, a jurisdiction may be eligible for both of the following:

  1. Administrative civil penalty relief for the 2022 calendar year pursuant to PRC section
  42652.5(d).
  2. A corrective action plan pursuant to 14 CCR section 18996.2.
  a. CalRecycle may address through a corrective action plan any violations disclosed in a
  jurisdiction’s notification that will take more than 180 days to correct. In this situation,
  the proposed actions and schedule in the jurisdiction’s approved notification will be in
  effect until a corrective action plan is issued.

CalRecycle will respond in writing to a jurisdiction within 45 business days of receiving its
notification with an approval, disapproval, request for additional information, or timeline for a
decision on approval or disapproval. CalRecycle will include details about why a jurisdiction did not
meet the requirements for a Notification of Intent to Comply when disapproving the jurisdiction’s
notification.

SUBJECT:  PUBLIC HEARING TO REVIEW AND CONSIDER  THE
  REDISTRICTING DRAFT MAPS RECOMMENDED BY  THE
  ADVISORY REDISTRICTING COMMISSION
ISSUE
Public Hearing to Review and Consider the Redistricting Draft Maps Recommended by
the Advisory Redistricting Commission.

RECOMMENDATION
The City Council has the following options:
  1. Approve one of the two proposed district boundary maps (Public Map 208 and
  ALVA Map) recommended by the Advisory Redistricting Commission and direct
  staff to bring back Ordinance No. 1579, An Ordinance of the City Council of the
  City of Palmdale Adopting a Map Describing Voting District Boundaries and
  Amending Chapter 4.10 of Title 4 of the Palmdale Municipal Code at the
  February 16, 2022 City Council meeting.

  2. Reject both proposed district boundary maps and return it to the Advisory
  Redistricting Commission with a detailed statement of the reasons for such
  disapproval and a request to modify the proposed district boundary maps for
  future consideration by the Advisory Redistricting Commission.

BACKGROUND
Every ten years, California cities with by-district election systems must use new census
data to review and, if needed redraw district lines to reflect how local populations have
changed. This process, called redistricting, ensures all districts have nearly equal
population. The redistricting process for the City of Palmdale must be completed
by April 17, 2022.

The City of Palmdale adopted its current district boundaries in 2016 based on 2010
census data, as required by law. The district boundaries must now be reconsidered using
the 2020 census data and in compliance with the Fair and Inclusive Redistricting for
Municipalities and Political Subdivisions (“FAIR MAPS”) Act, which was adopted by the
 Report to Mayor and City Council

Redistricting Commission

California legislature as AB 849 and took effect January 1, 2020.  AB 1276 is a
subsequent clean up of AB 849 and took effect on January 1, 2021.

FAIR MAPS ACT and REDISTRICTING REQUIREMENTS:
Under the Act, the City shall draw and adopt district boundaries using the following
criteria, in the listed order of priority (See, California Elections Code §21621, et. al.):

  1) Comply with the federal requirements of equal population and the Voting Rights
  Act;
  2) Geographically contiguous;
  3) Undivided neighborhoods and “communities of interest” (socio-economic
  geographic areas that should be kept together);
  4) Easily identifiable boundaries;
  5) Geographic compactness (do not bypass one group of people to get to a more
  distant group of people); and,
  6) Shall not favor or discriminate against a political party.

Once the prioritized criteria are met, other traditional districting principles can be
considered, such as:

  1) Minimize the number of voters delayed from voting in 2022 to 2024;
  2) Respect voters’ choices / continuity in office; and
  3) Future population growth.

By law, the City must hold at least four public hearings that enable community members
to provide input on the drawing of district boundary maps:

    At least one public hearing must be held before the City Council or Advisory
  Redistricting Commission draws a draft map or maps of the proposed district
  boundaries;
    At least two of the public hearings shall be held after the City Council or
  Advisory Redistricting Commission has drawn a draft map or maps of the
  proposed district boundaries; and
    At least one public hearing or public workshop shall be held on a Saturday, on
  a Sunday, or after 6 p.m. on a weekday Monday through Friday.

To increase the accessibility of these hearings, the City of Palmdale must additionally
take the following steps:

    At least one public hearing or public workshop shall be held on a Saturday, on
  a Sunday, or after 6 p.m. on a weekday Monday through Friday;
    Public hearings shall be accessible to persons with disabilities; and
    If a public hearing is consolidated with a regular or special meeting of the

DISCUSSION
The purpose of this public hearing is to have the City Council consider the two
recommended district boundary maps (Public Map 208 and ALVA Map) made by the
Advisory Redistricting Commission in accordance with Resolution No. CC 2021-031,
which states, in part:
  SECTION 13. Schedule. The Commission shall forward its final
  recommendation regarding a proposed district map to the City Clerk by
  no later than January 21, 2022. Upon receipt of the recommendation,
  the City Clerk shall immediately cause the recommended map(s) to be
  published for a seven-day public review period. Thereafter, the City
  Council shall conduct a public hearing on the Commission proposed
  map(s). At this hearing the City Council may elect to: (1) direct staff
  to introduce an ordinance approving one of the Commission
  recommended  maps/sequencing  or  (2)  reject  the

In accordance with the Resolution, the City Council may consider either proposed

OPTION #1 - ADOPT A PROPOSED DISTRICT BOUNDARY MAP:
Should the City Council choose to adopt one of the two proposed district boundary
maps (Public Map 208 or ALVA Map) recommended by the Advisory Redistricting
Commission, the Council will vote to direct staff to bring back an ordinance at the Fifth
Public Hearing on February 16, 2022 for introduction and formal adoption by the City
Council.

OPTION #2 - REJECT THE PROPOSED DISTRICT BOUNDARY MAPS:
Should the City Council choose to reject the two proposed district boundary maps
recommended by the Advisory Redistricting Commission, the Council must provide a
detailed statement of the reasons for such disapproval with a request to modify the
proposed district boundary or boundaries for future consideration by the Advisory
Redistricting Commission.

A Fifth Public Hearing is scheduled for February 16, 2022, at 7:30 p.m. to adopt the
final map ordinance, effective thirty days after City Council approval.

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE
  ESTABLISHING A REDISTRICTING COMMISSION PURSUANT TO
  ELECTIONS CODE SECTION 23000

  WHEREAS, members of the City Council of the City of Palmdale ("City") adopted
Ordinance No. 1471, transitioning from at-large to by-district city councilmember elections
under Elections Code § 10010; and

  WHEREAS, the City Council are currently elected in "district-based " election, in
which each city councilmember is elected only by the voters in the district in which the
candidate resides; and

  WHEREAS, Elections Code 21601 and 23000 authorizes the City Council to appoint
a redistricting Commission; and

  WHEREAS, the City Council desires to receive input on district boundaries from a
geographically diverse sector of the community; and

  WHEREAS, the Fair Maps Act (AB 849) became effective January 1, 2020 and
created standardized redistricting criteria aimed to keep communities together and to
prohibit partisan gerrymandering. The Act also expanded community outreach and public
hearing requirements and timelines, which coincide with the State redistricting schedule
(ATTACHMENT 1); and

  WHEREAS, the SB 1018 became effective on January 1, 2019 expanding the
methods for re-drawing district maps. Under this legislation, in addition to appointing an
advisory, or an independent commission, the City Council may instead elect to appoint a
hybrid commission or contract with Los Angeles County’s Citizen Redistricting
Commission (“CRC”), as outlined in the Authorities and Criteria for Redistricting
Commissions (ATTACHMENT 2) and provides for detailed information for each
commission):

  a. the City Council may adopt districts itself; and
  b. the City Council may appoint an advisory commission to recommend
  district boundaries for City Council adoption; and
  c. the City Council may establish an independent redistricting commission to
  adopt or new boundaries to the City; and
  d. the City Council may establish a hybrid redistricting commission to either
  adopt or recommend new boundaries to the City.

 NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the City of Palmdale, acting by and through
 its City Council, having considered and been fully advised in the matter and good cause
 appearing therefore does hereby resolve as follows:

 SECTION 1. Establishment. There shall be established the Palmdale Redistricting
 Commission, hereinafter "Commission" which shall be an Advisory Commission pursuant
 to Elections Code §23001. The Commission shall be established by June 1, 2021 and
 shall exist until the City Council adopts an ordinance establishing City Council district
 boundaries for the November 2022 election.

 SECTION 2. Membership. The Commission shall consist of 11 Commission members.
 Commission members shall consist of a diverse group of residents.

 SECTION 4. Selection Process. The Commission member selection process is
 designed to produce a qualified and impartial Commission. Commission members
 shall be selected through an open application process. Any person who meets the
 minimum Commission member qualifications in Section 5 may apply to serve on
 the Commission. Commissioners shall be appointed as follows

  A. The City Clerk shall initiate and widely publicize the Commission application
  process. To promote a large and diverse applicant pool, the City Clerk shall seek
  assistance from a broad range of community-based organizations to encourage
  qualified persons to apply. The application period shall be open through the
  earliest statutory date required.

  B. At the end of the application period, the City Clerk shall review and verify the
  information contained in each application, including applicants’ eligibility to serve
  on the Commission under Section 5. The City Clerk shall remove from the
  applicant pool any applicant who does not meet the minimum Commission
  member qualifications.

  C. The applicants may be considered taking into account the following factors:

  (1) The Commission should not be comprised entirely of members who are
  registered to vote with the same political party preference.

  (2) Commission members should reasonably reflect the City of Palmdale’s
  diverse geography and reside in diverse areas throughout the city.

  (3) Race/ethnicity may be considered without using formulas, quotas or
  ratios.

  (4) Gender, age, economic class, sexual orientation and party registration
  may be considered in selecting Commission members.

  (5) Commission members shall be impartial, know the jurisdiction’s
  neighborhoods and communities, appreciate the jurisdiction’s diversity and
  work well with others.

 SECTION 5. Eligibility Requirements for Members of the Commission. The
 application process shall be open to all eligible residents. The following

 A. A person, or the family member of a person (i.e., spouse, registered domestic

  (1) Been elected or appointed to, or been a candidate for, an elective

  (2) Served as an officer of, employee of, or paid consultant to, a campaign
  Commission or a candidate for elective office of Palmdale.

  (3) Served as an officer of, employee of, or paid consultant to, a political

  Commission.

  (4) Served as a staff member of, consultant to, or contracted with, a
  currently serving elected officer of Palmdale.

  (5) Been registered to lobby in Palmdale.

  (6) Contributed five hundred dollars ($500) or more in a year to any
  candidate for an elective office of Palmdale.

B. A member of the Commission shall not do any of the following:

  (1) While serving on the Commission, endorse, work for, volunteer for, or
  make a campaign contribution to, a candidate for an elective office of Palmdale.

  (2) Be a candidate for an elective office of Palmdale for 5 years commencing
  with the date of his or her appointment to the Commission.

  (3) For four years commencing with the date of his or her appointment to the
  Commission:

  a. Accept an appointment to a Palmdale Board, Commission or
  Commission.

  c. Receive a noncompetitively bid contract with Palmdale.

  d. Register as a lobbyist in Palmdale.

 C. Must be a resident of Palmdale and resided in Palmdale for at least the past

 D. Must be a registered voter. Those residents not eligible to vote due to age or citizenship

 SECTION 6. During and Post-Service Restrictions. Commission members shall comply
 with the following during and post-service restrictions as contained in California
 Elections Code Section 23003(d):

 A. While serving on the Commission, members may not work for, volunteer for, or
 make a campaign contribution to, a candidate for an elective office of Palmdale.

 B. Commission members may not run for an elective office of Palmdale for 5 years
 commencing with the date of my appointment to the Commission.

 C. For four years commencing with the date of his or her appointment to the
 Commission, members shall not:

  (1) Accept an appointment to a Palmdale Board, Commission or
  Commission.

  (2) Accept employment as a staff member of, or consultant to, an elected
  official or candidate for elective office of Palmdale.

  (3) Receive a noncompetitively bid contract with Palmdale.

  (4) Register as a lobbyist in Palmdale.

 SECTION 7. Redistricting Criteria. The Commission shall take into account the
 following legally required criteria in recommending district boundaries:

 A. Each city council district shall contain a nearly equal population;
 B. A redistricting plan shall be drawn in a manner that complies with the Federal Voting
  Rights Act, the California Voting Rights Act and the Equal Protection Clause of the
  U.S. Constitution; and

 C. City Council districts shall not be drawn with race as the predominate factor.

  freeways, creeks, railroad lines or other barriers) and communities of interest (school
  district boundaries, neighborhood boundaries, retail/commercial districts, voting

 SECTION 8. Public Transparency. The Commission shall implement an open process for

  A. The Commission members shall file Form 700 – Statement of Economic Interest

  C. The Commission shall comply with the California Public Records Act,
  commencing with Section 6250 of the California Government Code, and the
  Ralph M. Brown Act, commencing with Section 54950 of the California
  Government Code.

  D. The Commission shall publish on the internet and make available to the public
  a draft version of a proposed final map before final recommendation to the
  City Council.

  E. All records of the Commission relating to redistricting, and all data considered
  by the Commission in drawing a draft map or proposed final map, are public
  records.

  F. The City shall establish and make available to the public on the internet a
  calendar of all public hearings.

  G. The City shall establish and maintain for ten years a webpage for the
  Commission where important redistricting materials may be published,
  including hearing agendas, hearing minutes, links to hearing audio or video
  recordings where applicable, a Commission member roster, and draft maps
  created by the Commission.

  H. Commission members shall disclose all contact regarding the Commission's
  subject matter jurisdiction that occurs outside of a publicly noticed meeting.
  Commission members shall disclose these contacts no later than the
  Commission's next regular or special meeting.

  I. Any person who is compensated for communicating with the Commission or
  any Commission member, other than a reimbursement of reasonable travel
  expenses, shall identify the party compensating them in such
  communication.

 SECTION 9. Public Engagement. The Commission and the City should actively
 encourage residents to participate in the redistricting process.

 Introduction
The City of Palmdale has launched an aggressive outreach effort to reach across the entire
Palmdale community to engage and educate the public about the redistricting process. This
Outreach Summary Report is intended to provide a high-level overview of the outreach
philosophy, process and results to date.

Key highlights from these communication efforts include:
   Repeated email or phone contact with nearly 120 people and organizations to
  proactively outreach to key influencers, community leaders and community-based
  organizations with redistricting related information, including hearing agendas and
  meeting information.
   Rollout of the Redistricting website, DrawPalmdale.org, where extensive resources are
  available for the public to learn about the redistricting process, access all the materials
  and meeting information, and to draw maps based upon their understanding of
  communities of interest and submit them for consideration in the future.
   Flyers in English and Spanish to promote upcoming community meetings
   101 English and Spanish social media posts spread across Facebook, Instagram and
  Twitter from August through February.
  o Instagram – 30 posts
  o Facebook – 34 posts
  o Twitter – 37 posts
   Billboard that reads “Send Your Map”
   Radio commercials on Spanish radio talk show, including 1410 am and 1470 am
   Magazine advertisements in Palmdale Magazine in Palmdale Connections
  o Palmdale Magazine - Summer 2021, Fall 2021 and Winter/Spring 2022
  o Palmdale Connections - Jan/Feb 2022, Nov/Dec. 2021, Sept/Oct. 2021
   Press releases in English and Spanish distributed to the City’s media contacts. The
  redistricting process was featured 14 times by external news sources, including The
  Antelope Valley Times and Antelope Valley Press.

  3
 A Unique Timeline Challenge
The redistricting process that was triggered by the 2020 Census is unique as a result of the
delay in release of the Census data. In normal years, the Census data would become available
in April of the year after the Census (April 2021), but due primarily to the impact of the
Coronavirus Pandemic, the data release was delayed. The federal government released the
2020 Census data on August 12, 2021. However, the FAIR MAPS Act requires California to
adjust the census data by reassigning state and county prisoners to their last known address.
The official data from the State of California that cities are required to use for the redistricting
process was released on September 16, 2021. After several modifications, the data was ready
for the public to use in early October.

The delayed data release has compressed the redistricting process in hundreds of agencies
across California. To address this challenge, the City of Palmdale launched a process to engage
and inform the public early with redistricting information and prepare them to participate in
the process once the official data was released and map drawing had commenced.

Building an Outreach Team
The City of Palmdale built a team of professionals to effectively execute the community
outreach component of the project. This team included City of Palmdale staff, Tripepi Smith
and National Demographics Corporation (NDC). These parties met jointly on regular calls to
discuss the project and coordinate efforts. The integration of the demographer (NDC) into the
outreach plan was designed to ensure that communications properly contributed to the
broader goals of public information and drawing maps. This team approach helped eliminate
silos of knowledge in this critical project, made more important by the challenging compressed
timeline.

Tripepi Smith was engaged as an outreach expert on the redistricting process. The firm has a
long history of collaboration with NDC and has worked with other cities to assist with their
migration to district elections. During this redistricting cycle, the firm is working with over 20
other cities and counties on their redistricting outreach.

These outreach efforts were ably assisted by the City Clerk’s team and the Communications
team for the City of Palmdale.

 Community Workshops
The City of Palmdale held a series of four Redistricting Community Workshops to engage the
public and seek input on communities of interest.

October 12, 2021 – District 1, Holiday Inn
October 16, 2021 – District 4, Knight High School
October 16, 2021 – District 3, Palmdale Oasis Park Recreation Center
October 25, 2021 – District 2, Marie Kerr Park Recreation Center

To ensure most residents had the opportunity to participate, each community workshop gave
residents the option to attend in person at the listed locations or virtually via Zoom. National
Demographics Corporation was present at each meeting to educate residents on the
redistricting process and answer questions. Tripepi Smith facilitated each of the workshops
and encouraged residents to engage in dialogue related to neighborhoods and communities of
interest.

  Good afternoon,

  The City of Palmdale is in the midst of its redistricting process and the City Council needs your help to draw new district
  lines for the purposes of electing a City Council Member.

  Redistricting is the process where district lines for Congress, State Legislatures, County Board of Supervisors, City
  Councils, School Boards and other elected officials are redrawn every 10 years based on Census data. New district maps
  must be drawn to ensure districts have an equal number of constituents and fair representation among all residents.

  On behalf of the City of Palmdale, we are asking organizations and community members to spread the word about
  redistricting to their friends, neighbors and colleagues and get involved in the process by attending public meetings and
  submitting draft maps or public comments.
